# From a point flash to a track segment {#sec-cone-segment}

Everything so far started from a flash: light released at one place, at one
time, in one direction or in all of them. A particle does not oblige. It
travels, it radiates as it goes, and what it radiates leaves at a fixed angle
to its path. This chapter turns the point-source machinery into the response
to a straight Cherenkov segment of finite length, and then to a small event
made of several such segments — without solving the transport equation again
even once.

The claim that nothing new has to be solved needs proof, not assertion, so
this chapter also builds an independent control for the result and reports
what it found, including one thing it found the hard way.

## The cone is a source, not a new equation {#sec-cone-source}

A particle at $\mathbf x_0$ moving along the unit vector $\mathbf u$ with
speed $\beta c$ radiates, per unit path, into the cone of directions at fixed
angle $\theta_C$ to $\mathbf u$,

$$
\cos\theta_C=\mu_C=\frac1{\beta n_{\rm ph}},
$$ {#eq-cone-angle}

uniformly in azimuth. Note which index appears: $n_{\rm ph}$, the **phase**
index, sets the angle, while the photons then travel at the group speed
$c/n_{\rm g}$. Mixing the two is one of the easiest mistakes to make here,
and the code keeps them as separate inputs for that reason.

Write the emission as a direction density normalised over the sphere,
$$
p_C(\mathbf s)=\frac{\delta(\mathbf s\cdot\mathbf u-\mu_C)}{2\pi}.
$$

The response to one emission point is then the directed point response of
@sec-spatial averaged over that density. That average is where the work
disappears, because of one identity: for any two unit vectors and any degree,

$$
\int p_C(\mathbf s)\,P_l(\widehat{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathbf s)\,\mathrm d\Omega
=P_l(\mu_C)\,P_l(\widehat{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathbf u).
$$ {#eq-cone-addition}

This is the addition theorem again, in the same role it played in
@sec-om-acceptance: averaging a Legendre polynomial over a cone of directions
about $\mathbf u$ multiplies it by $P_l$ of the cone angle. The azimuthal
integral is done, exactly, once and for all.

So the once- and multiply-scattered response of a cone element at $a$ along
the track, seen by an isotropic point receiver at $\mathbf R$, is

$$
\boxed{
\widehat N^{(p)}(\omega)=y\int_0^{h}\mathrm da\;
e^{i\omega\left(t_0+a/\beta c\right)}
\sum_{l=0}^{J}M^{(p)}_l\bigl(r(a),\omega\bigr)\,
P_l(\mu_C)\,P_l\bigl(\widehat{\mathbf r}(a)\cdot\mathbf u\bigr),}
$$ {#eq-segment-orders}

with $y$ the yield per metre in the band the cache was built for, $p$ running
over the scattered orders, $r(a)=|\mathbf R-\mathbf x_0-a\mathbf u|$ and
$\widehat{\mathbf r}(a)$ the unit vector along it. The $M_l$ are exactly the
cached multipole moments of @eq-cache-moments. **Moving, rotating or
re-timing the segment changes only the arguments $r(a)$, the cosine and the
phase.** The transport solve behind $M_l$ never sees any of it.

Three things in @eq-segment-orders are worth naming explicitly, because each
is a place where a shortcut would be tempting and wrong. The time in the
exponent is the emission time of *that* element, $t_0+a/\beta c$, so a long
segment is never collapsed to a single emission time. The distance is the
distance from *that* element, not from a midpoint. And the angular factor is
evaluated at the true $\widehat{\mathbf r}(a)\cdot\mathbf u$, which swings
through a wide range along a segment that passes close to the receiver.

## The unscattered light is a Jacobian {#sec-segment-ballistic}

The unscattered term is not part of @eq-segment-orders and must not be: for a
point receiver it is a $\delta$-function in the emission variables, and the
cache never sees it. It has an exact closed form.

Put the receiver at distance $b$ from the track axis and $z$ along it,
measured from the segment start. A photon emitted at $a$ reaches it without
scattering only if the direction $\mathbf R-\mathbf x(a)$ lies on the cone,
which happens at exactly one point,

$$
a_*=z-\frac{b\,\mu_C}{\sin\theta_C},
\qquad
d_*=\frac{b}{\sin\theta_C},
$$ {#eq-ballistic-root}

and only if $0\le a_*<h$. The fluence follows from the $\delta$ in $p_C$
against the $1/d^2$ spreading of the flight,

$$
\boxed{
Q_0=\frac{y\,e^{-\mu_t d_*}}{2\pi\,b\,\sin\theta_C},
\qquad
t_0^{\rm arr}=t_0+\frac{a_*}{\beta c}+\frac{d_*\,n_{\rm g}}{c}.}
$$ {#eq-ballistic-fluence}

Two features deserve attention. The result falls as $1/b$, not $1/b^2$: a
line source seen through a cone concentrates light onto a ring, and the
exponent is the one-dimensional one. And the attenuation is the full $\mu_t$
over the flight $d_*$, not $\mu_a$ — this is the unscattered term, and any
scattering removes a photon from it.

The interval is half-open, $0\le a_*<h$, so that splitting a segment at any
interior point counts the junction once. That convention is what makes the
additivity test below exact rather than approximately exact.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Counting rays through a small sphere"}
@eq-ballistic-fluence was checked by an estimate that shares no factor with
it: emission points and cone azimuths are sampled, each ray is tested
geometrically for passage through a sphere of radius $\rho$ around the
receiver, and the accepted weight $e^{-\mu_t d}$ is divided by $\pi\rho^2$.
Shrinking $\rho$ must converge to the point-receiver value.

Because only a narrow band of azimuths and emission points can hit a small
sphere, the sampler restricts both to windows around the ones aimed at the
receiver and carries the window widths in the weight. The windows are an
importance-sampling device, not an assumption; the routine reports the
fraction of accepted rays that landed near a window rim, and a nonzero
fraction means the answer is a lower bound rather than an estimate. That
diagnostic earned its keep immediately: at $\rho=0.2\,\mathrm m$ on a tilted
segment it flagged $29\%$ of hits at the rim and the estimate came out
$12\%$ low, while at $\rho\le0.05\,\mathrm m$ the flag was zero and the
agreement was within one standard error.
:::

## The independent control, and what it cost {#sec-segment-independent}

The scattered orders of @eq-segment-orders reuse the cached moments, the
$k$ quadrature, the taper, the radial interpolation and the truncation at
$L$. A check that reuses any of them proves nothing about them. So the
control is built in coordinate space, from the three things a
once-scattered photon does:

$$
K_1(\omega)=y\int_0^h\!\!\mathrm da\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\frac{\mathrm d\varphi}{2\pi}
\int_0^\infty\!\!\mathrm dd\;
\mu_s\,e^{-\mu_t d}\,p\!\left(\cos\theta_s\right)
\frac{e^{-\mu_t \ell}}{\ell^2}\,
e^{i\omega\left(t_0+a/\beta c+(d+\ell)/v\right)},
$$ {#eq-segment-control}

where the photon leaves the element at $a$ along the cone ray of azimuth
$\varphi$, scatters once at distance $d$, and covers $\ell$ to the receiver.
No multipoles, no Bessel functions, no Fourier inversion, no interpolation.

The kernel $p$ is available in two forms, and using the right one is the
whole point of the exercise. With the full Henyey-Greenstein kernel,
@eq-segment-control is what nature does. With the kernel truncated at the
solver's own $L$,
$$
p_L(x)=\sum_{l\le L}\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}g^l P_l(x),
$$
it is what the finite-$L$ solver is *trying* to compute. Comparing against
the first isolates nothing; comparing against the second isolates everything
except the angular truncation, which the two kernels then measure on their
own. @sec-om-isotropic quotes the resulting separation for a directed point
flash; the same machinery drives it for a segment.

::: {.callout-important title="The lesson that cost the most time"}
For a receiver the cone reaches ballistically, @eq-segment-control has an
integrable singularity, and a product rule in $(a,\varphi)$ does not converge
against it. The reason is physical: photons that scatter by a vanishing angle
just before the receiver arrive from rays passing arbitrarily close to it, so
the inner integral behaves as $1/\rho$ with $\rho$ the distance to the
ballistic emission point and azimuth in @eq-ballistic-root. The integral
converges, since the area element in the plane supplies another factor of
$\rho$; a tensor Gauss rule does not.

Three quadratures were tried. A product rule in $(a,\varphi)$ drifted:
$5.72$, $5.25$, $4.87$ in units of $10^{-3}$ as the order rose — moving
steadily, converging to nothing. A rule in arrival directions at the
receiver, which cancels the $1/\ell^2$ analytically, drifted the same way
because the unscattered cone field it needs is itself ridged along the track.
What works is polar coordinates centred on the singular point, whose Jacobian
cancels the $1/\rho$ exactly, with the azimuth first rescaled into a
transverse distance so that one polar radius means the same thing along both
axes. That converges to seven digits by order $24$: $3.0465664$,
$3.0466247$, $3.0466359$, $3.0466364\times10^{-3}$.

The lesson generalises past this integral. A slowly drifting quadrature is
not a converging one, and the fix is almost never more nodes.
:::

### What the comparison says {#sec-segment-numbers}

With the reference converged — its own refinement moves it by $10^{-8}$ to
$3\times10^{-5}$, below every difference quoted — the cached route stands at:

| geometry | cone reaches it | difference |
|---|---|---:|
| short segment, receiver just off the cone | no, root at $2.53$ m past a $2$ m segment | $6.4\times10^{-3}$ |
| short segment, receiver behind | no | $5.4\times10^{-7}$ |
| long segment, receiver on the cone | yes | $2.8\times10^{-5}$ |
| long segment, receiver behind | no | $2.2\times10^{-7}$ |
| long segment, far receiver | no | $6.3\times10^{-5}$ |
| tilted slow segment, receiver on the cone | yes | $6.6\times10^{-3}$ |
| tilted slow segment, receiver behind | no | $1.1\times10^{-6}$ |

The pattern is not random. The cached route is at its best when the receiver
is nowhere near the cone surface, and at its worst when the receiver sits on
it or just off it — the same near-singularity in $\nu\to1$ that made the
control hard to integrate is the feature the multipole sum has to resolve.
Raising $L$ does not help: at the worst geometry, $L=32\to64$ at fixed spatial
settings changes the answer by $10^{-6}$, while raising $k_{\max}$ from $10$
to $24\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ moves the difference from $-0.9\%$ through $-0.6\%$ to
$+0.3\%$. The cost of that last setting is real: the same cache took $491$ s
to build instead of $37$.

Two more comparisons, on the lit long segment: at nonzero frequency the
complex difference is $2.9\times10^{-5}$ at $\omega=0.05$ and
$6.8\times10^{-5}$ at $0.2\,\mathrm{ns^{-1}}$, so nothing degrades with the
time structure; and the prototype's longitudinal quadrature needs more nodes
there than elsewhere — $16$ nodes give $7\times10^{-3}$, $32$ give
$2.8\times10^{-5}$, and past that it stops moving. Geometries the cone misses
are converged at $16$.

A sampled control runs alongside it, with the volume element written as
$\ell^2\,\mathrm d\ell\,\mathrm d\Omega_n$ about the receiver so that the
$1/\ell^2$ cancels, sampling arrival directions uniformly and $\ell$
exponentially. It shares no variable with @eq-segment-control. It agrees to a
few parts in a thousand and no better, and the reason is worth recording: the
unscattered cone field carries a $1/b$ ridge along the track, which gives the
estimator a logarithmically divergent variance. Its batch spread therefore
understates its own uncertainty, and it is quoted here as a
cross-check at the per-mille level, not as a precision reference.

## A small event, in three poses {#sec-segment-event}

An event is a sum. Each segment carries its own start, direction, length,
$\beta$, start time and yield; the receiver array stays where it is. Because
@eq-segment-orders only ever asks the cache for $M_l(r,\omega)$, the same
cache answers the original event, a translated copy and a rotated copy.

The demonstration in `scripts/run_segment_event.py` is eight segments — a
primary that changes direction twice, plus five delayed branches — read by
fourteen receivers on two strings. Four invariances are checked by
recomputing, never by construction:

* rotating and translating event and receivers together must change nothing;
* delaying the whole event by $\Delta t$ must multiply the spectrum by
  $e^{i\omega\Delta t}$;
* doubling every yield must double every component;
* splitting a segment in half, with the second half starting at the time the
  particle arrives there, must reproduce the whole.

The first three hold to the floating-point level, the fourth to the accuracy
of the longitudinal quadrature. A fifth check is negative on purpose: a
receiver outside the cached radial range must raise, not quietly return zero.

Time bins need one distinction. Orders $1$ and $\ge2$ are inverted from the
spectrum on a finite frequency window, which produces ringing and negative
bins near sharp features; those are kept as computed, because clipping them
hides exactly the diagnostic that says the window is too narrow. Order $0$ is
not inverted at all: @eq-ballistic-fluence gives its charge and its arrival
time exactly, so it is placed in the bin that contains that time.

## What this does not yet do {#sec-segment-limits}

The receiver here is an isotropic point. A directional module in front of a
*directed* source is the case @sec-om-limits already flagged as unimplemented,
and a Cherenkov cone is a directed source; the combination needs the $m\ne0$
blocks.

The $\ge2$ order has no independent control. It inherits the checks of
@sec-numerical-scheme through the cache, and it passes the invariance and
splitting tests above, but nothing here recomputes it from a different
construction. Saying so is part of the result.

One wavelength, one constant $\beta$ per segment, no spectral weighting of
$n_{\rm ph}$, and no conversion from a real shower's step list: those are the
next pieces, and each of them is a place where an average would be easy and
wrong.
